title: Focusability of <video> and <audio> and possible spec gap
body:
I've been conducting a review of changes to HTML on behalf of the W3C Accessible Platform Architectures Working Group, and have some questions about 15cf23a: it looks like a gap may have opened up in the spec as to whether `<audio controls>` and `<video controls>` elements should be in the focus order. (Their browser-provided controls are specced to be focusable, but this question is about the elements themselves.)

We would also like to explore what the focusability of these elements should be (more on that below).

#### Possible spec gap

I may have missed something, but here's what I found...

* The [HTML 5.2 CR recommends `<audio controls>` and `<video controls>` should be in the focus order by default](https://www.w3.org/TR/html52/editing.html#the-tabindex-attribute) (scroll down to "If the attribute is omitted or parsing the value returns an error"); the changes made in 15cf23a here effectively take them out of that list ([latest list of default-focusable elements](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html#dom-tabindex)).
* There is the [definition of "interactive content"](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dom.html#interactive-content), which states that `<audio controls>` and `<video controls>` are interactive, though doesn't explicitly state that interactive content must be placed in the focus order. (Though it would seem reasonable.)
* The [table about focusable areas states that browser-provided controls should be focusable](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html#td-fa-3) but it does not say that the `<audio controls>` and `<video controls>` elements themselves should be in the focus order.

Do you think the spec is sufficiently clear on this? (I defer to your judgement.)

#### Should the media elements themselves be focusable?

We thought it would be a good idea to have a community discussion about this. Before we discuss that question, though: what are the options for the browser-provided controls?

* Either implement each embedded control as separate element, so the buttons and sliders would each take one focus order slot, or
* implement the set of controls as a toolbar, which takes one tab stop and uses the arrow keys to navigate between individual controls.

I feel the first option is simpler, easier to use and more web-like (it's also mostly how browsers implement them—more details below). However it seems that, as long as there is a way to interact with those controls via the keyboard, that is OK and shouldn't be (and isn't) mandated by the spec.

But what about the `<audio>` and `<video>` elements themselves—should they be in the focus order?

Some arguments in favour of making them focusable:

* It gives the user the opportunity to press <kbd>Space</kbd> to quickly play/pause the media. (Browsers may allow the user to click/tap on the video to play/pause it.)
* It sort-of matches how Firefox and Chrome work (details below).

Some arguments against making them focusable:

* It's an extra focus order stop (verbosity/time requirement).
* Focusing them or their controls could be inconsistent between `<audio>` and `<video>` elements, as videos take up space on-screen and may act as a big play/pause button themselves, but browsers may render only the playback controls for `<audio controls>` elements. (However I note an observation I've seen during my review that it's probably best to avoid assuming/prescribing rendering.)

In order to get around the problem of potentially ambiguous control labels, it was suggested that the `<audio controls>` and `<video controls>` could be exposed in the accessibility tree as containers, and use the label of the media element to disambiguate the labels for the embedded controls (i.e. all of the embedded "play" buttons may be called "Play/Pause" but the label for the containing media element could be used to disambiguate). This would be like a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`—a screen-reader could announce the legend text when the user first tabs into a `<fieldset>` to provide context. This could be of particular help if the media elements weren't in the focus order.

There's an additional option, which is a little bit how Chrome works:

Don't include the media elements themselves in the focus order (meaning that the browser-provided play button would be the first element, and the media could be treated like a container, as above), but if the user clicks or taps on the rendered media, then delegate that click/tap to the play/pause button. (Browsers could still choose to render a large play/pause symbol on top of the media when appropriate, though in order to be accessible, it should mirror the state of the "real" play/pause button.)

#### Current situation (quick test)

A quick test on Windows 10 with NVDA 2019.2.1 yielded the following results when examining the [MDN `<video>` example](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/video) and [MDN `<audio>` example](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/audio). Of note is that the `<audio>` example uses a figure and caption to give the media element a name, but the `<video>` example doesn't. NVDA announced the name associated with the `<audio>` element.

Firefox 70:

* Puts the `<video>` element in the focus order when first drawn (with embedded controls visible).
* All of the embedded controls are announced when the `<ideo>` element is focused.
* A play button is drawn over the centre of the video, distinct from the controls below.
* Only the full-screen button from the embedded controls bar is in the focus order.
* If the mouse hovers over the video and then leaves it, and the controls disappear, it is not possible to focus the `<video>` any more, nor restore the controls.
* All of the playback controls for the `<audio>` element were announced together, but this happened twice, which indicates that the `<audio>` element and the embedded controls set are each given focus order stops.
* Pressing <kbd>Space</kbd> when focused on the first `<audio>` tab stop didn't play the audio; pressing <kbd>Tab</kbd> and then space, to focus the second related tab stop, did play the audio.

Chrome 78:

* Puts the `<video>` element in the focus order when first drawn (with embedded controls visible).
* All of the embedded controls are announced when the `<ideo>` element is focused.
* For both `<audio>` and `<video>` elements, the play button in the controls bar is not announced the first time it gets focus, but is announced when the user travels back to it.
* Pressing <kbd>Space</kbd> when the whole `<video>` element is focused starts the video playing and moves the focus to the play/pause button in the embedded controls.
* The controls disappear when the video is playing, after a while, but re-appear when it finishes playing.
* For `<audio>` elements, the whole toolbar is announced only once; after that the individual controls are explored (with the "play" button not being announced the first time it's visited, as above).

In both browsers, the `<video>`'s filename was not announced as its accessible name, even though no other was provided. The `<figcaption>` was used as the accessible name for the audio.

In summary: it seems there are some accessibility issues, so this could be clouding the results.

#### Next steps

1. Decide if the spec is clear enough as-is.
2. Decide what the focusability of the elements should be.

Some discussion and perhaps user and browser-/AT-developer surveys may be of help in deciding what the behaviour should be.
